Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA View image in fullscreen An estimated 514 people have been arrested in France this summer on suspicion of starting wildfires. Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA France Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them? Experts believe one-third of wildfires in France are set deliberately, with arson the biggest single cause of forest fires last year Jon Henley in Paris Sun 13 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 03.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O ne is a boy of 15, who threw a burning cigarette into a wood near Bordeaux. Another is a 36-year-old man who set a paper bag of rubbish on fire in bushes near Perpignan. A third is a 50-year-old woman accused of lighting 17 fires south of La Rochelle. According to the French interior ministry, since the start of a summer in which a record 115,000 hectares of forest, scrub and heathland have gone up in flames, 514 people – including 198 minors – have been arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires . Who are they, and what motivates them? Experts say arson is an under-studied field in France . It remains, according to Thierry Toutin, a criminology researcher with the national police, “a mysterious crime, often hard for people to understand”. View image in fullscreen The summer of wildfires has turned the spotlight in France on the question of what – and who – is causing them. Photograph: Steph Picture/VHP/AFP/Getty Images Two hundred years ago, under Napoleon, deliberately starting a wildfire in France was a crime so grave it carried an automatic death penalty by guillotine. These days, sentences start at 10 years in jail and a €150,000 fine, rising to 15 years if protected forests or reserves burn, and life if someone is killed. Arsonists have “many different profiles”, Toutin said in an essay for The Conversation . Several French departments have set up dedicated arson groups uniting police, forestry board experts and local services to help identify, find and prosecute them, he said, but still: “These are often crimes that are unsolved, or don’t lead to convictions, because the fire has destroyed the evidence.” France’s official statistics classify wildfires by their cause: natural, such as lightning; accidental (say, a vehicle fire or electrical fault); involuntary professional (sparks from a machine); involuntary individual (a cigarette or barbecue) – and voluntary. In practice, as a government PSA has repeated all summer on radio, TV and online, nine out of 10 fires are caused by human activity, with roughly two-thirds classed as involuntary (which, if negligence is proven, carries a jail term of one to five years). That means fully one-third of wildfires in France each year are set deliberately, with the intention of doing harm. In 2025, the last year for which full figures are available, deliberate acts of arson were the biggest single cause of forest fires in France , accounting for 29.4% of blazes. Graph of the area of land burnt by wildfires in France Among those convicted this summer are a 27-year-old man diagnosed with autism and schizophrenia who set fire to a letter to his late daughter in tinder-dry vegetation near Béziers. He was sentenced to four years of detention and treatment. Perpignan court last week sentenced a 51-year-old man to five years in prison for lighting four fires in July and August. In Les Sables d’Olonnes, a volunteer firefighter – reported to police by his superiors – was handed a three-year suspended sentence. In Lyon, a 29-year-old man with a police record for theft, trafficking and domestic violence was convicted of setting a fire that destroyed more than a hectare of land, took 71 firefighters to extinguish and forced the evacuation of 150 people. View image in fullscreen Among those convicted of arson this summer is a volunteer firefighter. Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP Those convicted of negligence include a motorist who lit a fire to alert emergency services after he broke down (six months, suspended) and two restaurant owners in the south-west who defied a red fire alert to light a charcoal grill and set off fireworks. An early analysis based on police reports and obtained by Le Figaro showed 97.5 % of arson suspects arrested this year have been men, aged on average 32.5, with 28.7% under 18. More than 95% were French citizens. Of a relatively small sample of 80 suspects, 37 were unemployed. Exactly what drove them to act is often much harder to establish. In principle, criminologists identify four main categories of motivation. Some arson attacks are carried out in the context of a conflict: a dispute with a neighbour; criminal rivalry between gangs; revenge against someone or something. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Other arsonists may act for financial gain, such as a false insurance claim, or out of ideological or political conviction. The remainder display some kind of pathology, often psychological – including a small number of genuine pyromaniacs. “Arsonists may be after money, or revenge, or be trying to cover up a crime. They may be under the influence of alcohol or other substances,” said Laurent Layet, a psychiatrist. “A pyromaniac’s sole objective is to set fire to something.” Pyromaniacs “have difficulty organising their personalities”, Layet told France Inter radio . “They are often impulsive, and they have trouble controlling their emotions. Often, they are quite isolated socially.” Classified as an impulse-control disorder, pyromania is characterised by “a fascination with fire, by a mounting tension before the act, and then a feeling of pleasure or relief immediately afterwards”, he said. But pyromaniacs are typically organised, aware of the consequences of their acts, and considered criminally responsible. View image in fullscreen In all, a record 115,000 hectares of forest, heath and scrubland have gone up in flames so far this year. Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images They also represent barely 5% of the people who deliberately set fires. Another equally small group are firefighters – mostly volunteers, very rarely professionals – who deliberately set fires for the glory that comes from extinguishing them. Over the years, France’s departmental fire services have set up filtering mechanisms to detect such personalities during the recruitment process, including psychological tests. They acknowledge that each year, some slip through the net. But the motivation of most people who deliberately light wildfires is rarely quite so clearcut. For many, it boils down to an ill-defined “act of defiance – to confront the system, and get pleasure from destroying other people’s property”, said Johanna Rozenblum, a clinical psychologist who works with the fire service. A strikingly large proportion of the arsonists she had dealt with had “marked antisocial profiles”, Rozenblum said . And in the case of minors, adolescent impulsiveness and frustration combine with “immaturity and internal revolt” to prevent them fully realising the devastating scale of the damage they risk doing. Beállítom Tudják, mi az a beruházási többletköltség-kompenzáció? Ha nem, akkor Vitézy Dávidnak van egy jó híre, a beruházási és közlekedési miniszter ugyanis erről tett közzé posztot vasárnap, miután a pénteki kormányszóvivői sajtótájékoztatón röviden már beszélt róla. A lényeg, hogy az állam 2023 végén egy szerződésmódosítással átvállalta az orosz–ukrán háború okozta építőipari áremelkedés és a kamatok emelkedése miatti többletterhek jelentős részét a koncessziós cégtől, vagyis az MKIF-től, ami önmagában legalább ötezer milliárd forinttal növelte meg a szerződés időtartama alatt kifizetendő összeget. Méghozzá úgy, hogy a koncessziós szerződést egyébként a háború kitörése után írták alá, azaz Vitézy szerint az lett volna a logikus, ha az ebből fakadó költségeket és kockázatokat a vállalkozó viselte volna az állam, vagyis az adófizetők helyett. Vitézy posztja szerint a magyar állam alig másfél évvel a szerződés megkötése után, 2023 decemberében, egy Rogán Antal által aláírt szerződésmódosítással vállalta át a többletterhek jelentős részét, miközben addig egyetlen négyzetméter új autópálya sem épült. Mindennek egy veszélyhelyzeti kormányrendelet ágyazott meg, amely kimondta: a háború elhúzódó gazdasági hatásai 2022 második felétől jelentkeztek, azok előre nem voltak láthatóak, és kellő gondossággal eljárva sem lehetett őket előre látni. Erre hivatkozva teremtettek lehetőséget szerződések módosítására is. A kormány az elmúlt években előszeretettel használta az orosz–ukrán konfliktust mindenféle kormányrendeletek megindoklásához, erre hivatkozva döntöttek arról is, hogy a bor után a pálinkából is adómentes céges ajándékot csináljon a kormány, szóval nagyon széles volt azon dolgok köre, amire rá lehetett húzni az ukrajnai helyzet miatt bevezetett veszélyhelyzetet. Az autópálya-koncesszió szerződésének módosítását is ez a rendelet tette lehetővé, ezt végül arra hivatkozva lépték meg, hogy az MKIF-nek jelentősen nőttek többek között a kamatterhei és a költségei. Vitézy szerint ugyanakkor ezzel több probléma is van. Egyrészt egy koncessziónak éppen az lenne a lényege, hogy ezeket a kockázatokat a szerződött partner viselje, ez a konstrukció viszont szerinte úgy lett kialakítva, hogy a nyereség a Mészáros–Szíjj duó vállalatánál maradjon, miközben a kockázatok jelentős részét az állam viseli. Másrészt pedig a koncessziós szerződést majdnem három hónappal a háború kitörése után írták alá, vagyis egy valódi koncessziós szerződés értelme pont az lett volna, hogy ezeket az ismert költségeket és kockázatokat a vállalkozó viselje az adófizetők helyett. „Ez a szerződés azonban nem így működött: ha bármi veszélyeztette Mészáros és Szíjj profitját, az állam azonnal lépett, és a kockázatokat magára vállalta. Eddig: a Tisza-kormány a szerződés átvizsgálása után egyértelműen bizonyítottnak látja, hogy ez a szerződés túlárazott és jogszerűtlen, ezért kezdeményeztük annak megszüntetését” – írta Vitézy. A Mészáros-féle koncessziós cég az elmúlt hetekben azért került a figyelem középpontjába, mert Vitézy augusztus közepén bejelentette, az előző kormány döntését visszavonva mégsem adja az MKIF-nek az M6-os autópálya üzemeltetését. Magyar Péter a döntés után kiposztolta, hogy „felkészül a 35 éves autópálya-koncesszió”, ami komoly üzengetést indított be a Fidesz és a Tisza-kormány között, pénteken pedig Magyar és Vitézy bejelentették: a kormány döntést hozott arról, hogy elindítja a koncesszió megszüntetését. Vitézy Dávid itt is elmondta, a kormány több szempontból jogszerűtlennek tartja a szerződést, és szerinte indokuk is lenne, hogy egyoldalúan elálljanak tőle, de mivel ez sok évig tartó jogvitához is vezethetne, tárgyalásokat kezdeményeznek a vállalattal, hogy közös megegyezéssel, a lehető leghamarabb felszámolhassák a koncessziót. https://www.dw.com/en/jordan-karak-churc.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Oaw3 Jordanian state media published surveillance video of the attack in the village of Hammoud in Karak Governorate Image: Al Mamlaka TV/AFP Advertisement A shooting at a church in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak left seven people dead and another 34 wounded on Friday, Jordan's public security director Obaidallah Maaytah said. What do we know so far? The shooting occurred at the Hammoud Church. The shooting reportedly occurred during a funeral. The attackers' identities and motives remain unclear. Two men opened fire on the funeral procession. A witness told Jordanian state media there were 150 to 200 people present at the church at the time of the shooting. Videos circulating online showed wounded people on the floor of the church covered in blood, but this footage cannot be verified by DW. Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said a group of "extremists" carried out the massacre. According to Jordanian outlet Roya News, Al-Faraya said authorities already possess the names of suspects behind the attacks but would not publicly disclose their identities as of now. Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said security forces have launched a probe into the attack. Jordan King Abdullah II: 'We will strike with an iron fist' Jordan King Abdullah II said "the terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation." "Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," Abdullah II said, adding, "We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation." Lebanese President Joseph Aoun , a Christian, also condemned the "heinous terrorist attack" in Jordan and expressed condolences to the victims. US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the news regarding the attack is "devastating." "Praying for the victims, their families and all those affected by this depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship," Waltz said. "Attacks on Christians continue to escalate worldwide and must be stopped." Gun attacks like the one on the church in Karak are rare in Jordan. Although Jordan is largely a Muslim-majority country of around 11.5 million people, there is a small Christian minority of a couple hundred thousand. The Karak region, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of Amman, has a significant Christian population. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Edna O’Brien pictured in 1976. Her 1960 novel The Country Girls was banned in Ireland, partly because ‘you can see the contours of the female form’ on the cover. Photograph: ITV/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Edna O’Brien pictured in 1976. Her 1960 novel The Country Girls was banned in Ireland, partly because ‘you can see the contours of the female form’ on the cover. Photograph: ITV/Shutterstock Ireland Banned books from Ireland’s room of ‘evil literature’ finally see the light of day Censored books spanning 1926-96 contained themes ‘likely to corrupt or deprave’, or references to contraception or violence Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent Fri 13 Nov 2026 09.25 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 13.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For almost a century, an Irish government building in the heart of Dublin has hosted a secret sanctum: the banned books room. The department of justice, on St Stephen’s Green, did not grant public access, because the shelves contained 12,000 books deemed indecent or obscene. It was a graveyard for titles condemned by the Censorship of Publications Board, a guardian of public morals which guillotined anything that smelled of sex or other corruptions. Harold Robbins was interred. So too Ian Fleming, Edna O’Brien , Brendan Behan , Oscar Wilde, DH Lawrence, JD Salinger, John Updike, Iris Murdoch , F Scott Fitzgerald and many more. View image in fullscreen Books previously banned in Ireland that were held at the department of justice are to be moved to the National Archives. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration Exhumation, however, is nigh. The entire collection is to be moved to the National Archives as part of the repeal of Ireland’s censorship laws. The censors’ notes, minutes and ledgers that detail why each book was banned will be made publicly available for the first time – a trove for researchers of social history and state control. “The censors prohibited works that they saw as contravening or subverting public morality – anything that was seen as unwholesome or suggestive of sexual immorality,” said Orlaith McBride, the director of the National Archives. “It was often just the innuendo of something that could have been perceived as likely to corrupt or deprave.” View image in fullscreen Notes and ledgers from Ireland’s Censorship of Publications Board are to be made available to the public at the National Archives. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration The volumes span 1926 to 1996 and encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. References to family planning, contraception and violence were likely to elicit bans, said McBride. So too did suggestive imagery, such as the cover of O’Brien’s groundbreaking 1960 novel, The Country Girls . “It’s very subtly done but you can see the contours of the female form. The issue wasn’t just the contents but the image,” McBride said. Banned titles included classics such as Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, Behan’s Borstal Boy and Lawrence’s Lady Chatterley’s Lover, as well as pulpy paperbacks with titles such as The Baby Doll Murders, A Doctor and his Mistress and Torrid Tale of a Wicked Town. Scholarly tomes such as Sexual Life in England Past and Present and arcane works such as The Collected Works of Pierre Louÿs, a Belgian poet of the early 20th century, also ended up in what was informally called the banned books room. View image in fullscreen Torrid titles? The banned books encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration The censorship board adopted a broad definition of indecent and obscene, said Brian Hughes, a history lecturer at the University of Limerick’s Mary Immaculate College. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “I think people would be very surprised seeing these books or reading some of these books to think that they were banned at all in the first place, because attitudes are quite different now. I think it suggests that certainly in terms of printed matter, the written word, there’s a much more liberal society. It is a more secular society as well; that’s part of it. But I think it’s a wider process of attitudes towards sex, sexuality changing.” In 1926, soon after independence, the nascent Irish Free State established the Committee of Evil Literature, a five-man panel tasked with protecting public morals. It recommended a strict system of vetting that led to the Censorship of Publications Board – which, for a time, was led by a Catholic priest – and an appeals board. The censors reviewed material that was submitted by members of the public and customs and revenue officers. They also sourced books through a subscription to the Times Book Club. View image in fullscreen Minutes of a meeting in 1959 of Ireland’s Censorship of Publications Board. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration. The periodicals and books that accumulated at what is now known as the department of justice, home affairs and migration will be moved after Christmas to the National Archives, where they will be conserved, catalogued and stored. “Many are first editions, and because of sheer age in a vulnerable state, so they won’t be available to the public,” said McBride. People could source them online “and in all good bookshops”, she said. The censors’ registers and notes, plus letters from the public and interest groups, were transferred this week, and are undergoing conservation in advance of becoming publicly available. McBride said: “They are the most interesting because they record the decisions and reveal the thinking behind the bans.” Explore more on these topics Ireland Censorship Europe Libraries news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
